records.title: Accuracy of ultrasound in diagnosing anterior talofibular ligament injury: a meta-analysis.
records.abstract: The anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) is the most frequently injured structure of the ankle joint. This meta-analysis evaluates the diagnostic accuracy of ultrasound for anterior talofibular ligament injury. We systematically searched for PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and Cochrane Library databases, with a search deadline of November 28,2025, and extract data related to diagnostic performance. A bivariate model was used to summarize the estimated values and construct a summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curve. Heterogeneity was evaluated using I² statistic, clinical applicability was assessed using Fagan's nomogram and likelihood ratio scatter plot, and potential publication bias was employing Deeks funnel plot asymmetry test. A total of 21 studies were included, evaluating 1248 patients. The meta-analysis results indicate that the pooled sensitivity of ultrasound examination is 0.93 (95% CI: 0.89-0.96), specificity is 0.86 (95% CI: 0.78-0.91), area under the SROC curve (AUC) is 0.95, diagnostic odds ratio (DOR) is 100.74 (40.08-253.19), positive likelihood ratio (PLR) is 5.86 (95% CI: 3.65-9.43), and negative likelihood ratio (NLR) is 0.09 (95% CI: 0.05-0.15). Subgroup analyses showed that specificity was higher when MRI was used as the reference standard (0.88) and in prospective studies (0.85), with particularly favorable performance observed in investigations of chronic injury. Ultrasound shows promise as a first-line screening modality with high sensitivity and specificity. Whether routine ultrasound triage translates into reduced MRI referrals and overall cost savings warrants prospective health-economic evaluation.

records.title: Does six weeks of neuromuscular training lead to fewer lower limb injuries in New Zealand Army recruits? A cluster RCT.
records.abstract: Neuromuscular training can help to prevent musculoskeletal injury among sports populations; however, it requires further investigation with military recruits. This study investigated whether six weeks of neuromuscular training, compared with usual training, leads to fewer lower limb injuries among New Zealand Army recruits undertaking basic training. This double-blind cluster-randomized controlled trial included army recruits from two consecutive intakes. Recruits received six weeks of neuromuscular or usual training two to five times per week. The primary outcome was incidence of lower limb injuries during basic training. Secondary outcomes included total health care encounters for injury, occupational endpoint achieved, and accumulated light-duty days because of injury. Participants were 248 recruits (228 males, 20 females, mean age 20.28 years). Cumulative injury incidence in the control and neuromuscular training groups was 63.2% and 52.8%, respectively (p = 0.10). There was no between-groups difference in average number of injuries per recruit (control, 1.31, intervention, 1.10, p = 0.22). Average total health care encounters for injury per recruit was higher in the control group (control, mean 4.83 intervention, mean 3.45, p = 0.041). No statistically significant difference was found in occupational endpoint achieved (p = 0.21). Accumulated light-duty days totaled 964 and 725 in the control and intervention groups respectively (p = 0.10). Simple, low-cost neuromuscular lower limb exercises did not change overall injury incidence but lowered number of health care encounters for injuries sustained by New Zealand Army recruits during basic training.

records.title: Effects of exercise-induced fatigue and lunge direction on racket-side lower-limb biomechanics during forward lunges in male badminton athletes.
records.abstract: This study examined the effects of exercise-induced fatigue and lunge direction on racket-side lower-limb biomechanics during forehand and backhand forward lunges in male badminton athletes. Twenty-four male athletes performed standardized three-step lunges before and after a combined sprint-interval running and maximal vertical-jump fatigue protocol. Three-dimensional kinematics were recorded using a Vicon motion-capture system, while ground reaction forces were recorded using force platforms. Lower-limb biomechanical analyses focused on the racket-side limb. Outcome variables included phase durations, joint kinematics and moments, center-of-mass (COM) velocity, ground reaction forces (GRFs), impulses, joint quasi-stiffness, and dynamic postural stability. Outcomes were analyzed using two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with prespecified biomechanical-domain- and effect-specific Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction. No statistically significant fatigue × direction interactions were detected after BH correction; however, given the limited statistical sensitivity for interaction effects, these findings should be considered inconclusive. Fatigue shortened braking duration, reduced recovery-phase COM velocity gain, braking-phase impulses, recovery-phase anteroposterior impulse, and selected joint ROMs, while increasing recovery-phase hip and knee quasi-stiffness. Backhand lunges showed greater secondary-impact GRF, higher DPSI, VSI and MLSI values, greater ankle dorsiflexion and inversion, and a greater knee extension moment than forehand lunges. Within the racket-side limb, fatigue induced a more constrained lunge strategy and reduced recovery-phase impulse generation and COM velocity increase. Backhand lunges showed greater impact loading, braking-phase force fluctuations, and ankle mechanical demands than forehand lunges.

records.title: Physical Examination of Chronic Ankle Instability: Current Concepts.
records.abstract: Chronic ankle instability is a common condition with a substantial public health burden. When non-operative treatment fails, surgery should address both the ligament injury and associated lesions. Their identification relies on a comprehensive physical examination, which remains challenging and has limited reproducibility. This narrative Current Concepts review summarizes the mechanical and structural physical examination findings, the clinical tests used to assess the lateral ligament complex, medial ligamentous structures, the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis, the subtalar joint, associated impingement lesions, and generalized joint hypermobility, that inform surgical planning. For the lateral ligament complex, the anterior drawer and talar tilt tests demonstrate high specificity but limited sensitivity. Modified maneuvers, including the anterolateral and reverse anterolateral drawer tests, may improve diagnostic accuracy. However, reported reliability and accuracy remain inconsistent, and no single test is both highly sensitive and specific, supporting a bilateral, comparative, multi-test examination. A secondary aim of this review is to evaluate how patient positioning influences examination feasibility. No single position enables complete assessment, and comparative reliability studies are lacking. Based on biomechanical rationale and clinical experience rather than comparative evidence, the prone position may offer practical advantages, allowing a lateral ankle view and isolated subtalar assessment, but these potential advantages have not been confirmed by comparative studies. Current best practice remains a systematic, bilateral examination using complementary tests while recognizing the limitations of each maneuver.

records.title: [Design and analysis of a serial ankle rehabilitation robot].
records.journal: Sheng Wu Yi Xue Gong Cheng Xue Za Zhi
records.abstract: To address the complex mechanism configurations, strong motion coupling, and control complexity associated with some existing ankle rehabilitation robots, a two-degree-of-freedom serial ankle rehabilitation robot with independent actuation is proposed. The robot is capable of providing single-degree-of-freedom training in plantarflexion/dorsiflexion and adduction/abduction, as well as compound motion training. A kinematic model of the spatial orthogonal 2R mechanism was established, and its kinematic performance was analyzed. Ankle posture coupling constraints were introduced to refine the workspace. A prototype of the rehabilitation robot was subsequently fabricated, and ankle angle-tracking experiments were conducted using a Vicon three-dimensional motion capture system. The results showed that the mechanism had no singular configurations within the physiological range of motion of the human ankle. The maximum condition number was 1.414. In the prototype experiments, the mean absolute error and root mean square error for plantarflexion/dorsiflexion were 1.443° and 1.650°, respectively. For adduction/abduction, the corresponding values were 0.789° and 1.005°. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed robot configuration for ankle rehabilitation and its favorable performance in tracking human ankle joint angles during robot-assisted motion.

records.title: [Posttraumatic ankle arthrofibrosis : Diagnosis, prevention and treatment].
records.abstract: Posttraumatic arthrofibrosis is a rare cause of painful motion loss after injury or surgery, with limited available evidence. Posttraumatic arthrofibrosis is characterized by painful, progressive stiffness with more than 30% loss of motion and no major radiographic abnormality. Reported rates range from 2% to 10% after ankle injuries to up to 73% after surgically treated fractures, while ankle-specific data on risk factors remain limited. The pathogenesis appears to involve transforming growth factor (TGF)-β, interleukin (IL)-1, and hypoxia-mediated capsular fibrosis. Arthrography remains the diagnostic gold standard according to the Goldman criteria. Magnetic resonance imaging may show capsular thickening ≥ 3 mm and stage-dependent signal changes. First-line treatment comprises physiotherapy, mobilization, and dynamic or static progressive orthoses. A mean 17° gain in total range of motion was reported with static progressive orthoses. In refractory stiffness, arthroscopic capsular release may be beneficial, with improvement of the American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society (AOFAS) score from 63.8 to 88.6, dorsiflexion from 1 to 19°, and acceptable motion in more than 80% of patients. Posttraumatic arthrofibrosis of the ankle is rare, underdiagnosed, and treatable. Early recognition and stepwise conservative treatment, followed by arthroscopic capsular release, may restore function. The evidence is based mainly on small level IV studies. Prospective studies are required.

records.title: [Sensorimotor insoles for musculoskeletal disorders : An evidence-based rapid review].
records.abstract: Sensorimotor foot orthoses (SMFOs) are designed to modulate afferent input through targeted plantar stimuli and thereby influence neuromuscular control mechanisms. This review aimed to provide an evidence-based assessment of their clinical effectiveness across different musculoskeletal conditions. We conducted a rapid review of randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews. We evaluated the available evidence for different orthotic concepts on an indication-specific basis using the GRADE approach. The strongest evidence was for symptomatic flexible pes planovalgus and patellofemoral pain syndrome, although no consistent superiority of SMFOs over conventional supportive foot orthoses was demonstrated. In patients with patellofemoral pain syndrome, randomized data showed significant improvements in pain and function with both SMFOs and conventional foot orthoses. For chronic ankle instability, the evidence regarding sensorimotor interventions is largely limited to mechanistic and indirect outcomes. Interpretation is further complicated because the textured insoles used in many studies do not match what is traditionally understood as SMFOs in German-speaking orthopedic practice. Evidence for SMFOs in nonspecific low back pain is even more limited and is characterized by heterogeneous findings. Based on the current literature, no clear superiority of sensorimotor orthotic concepts can be demonstrated for any specific diagnosis. However, this should not be interpreted as evidence of general ineffectiveness. SMFOs represent a therapeutic option within multimodal treatment strategies and should be prescribed according to the individual indication and patient-specific treatment goals.

records.title: A balancing act: Passive ankle exoskeletons alter neuromuscular function and postural stability during balance.
records.abstract: Spring-loaded passive ankle exoskeletons have the potential to modulate neuromuscular function during standing balance by altering the mechanical demands placed on the muscle-tendon units spanning the ankle joint. This study investigated the effect of exoskeleton assistance on postural stability and neuromuscular function across balance conditions of varying difficulty. We hypothesised that assistance would improve postural stability and reduce ankle plantar flexor muscle activity during balance tasks, although these benefits may vary with balance task complexity. Participants performed standing balance tasks of varying difficulty with and without rotational stiffness provided by spring-loaded ankle exoskeletons. Balance tasks included (i) quiet standing with eyes open (EO), (ii) eyes closed (EC), and (iii) reduced base of support (RBOS). We recorded centre of pressure (COP)-based postural sway measures, lower limb joint kinematics, muscle activation data from the medial (MG) and lateral gastrocnemii (LG), soleus (SOL), and tibialis anterior (TA), and MG fascicle behaviour. Exoskeleton assistance reduced LG and SOL activation but also altered joint kinematics and coordination. Ankle-based adjustments were most evident with assistance during simpler balance tasks (EO and EC), whereas assistance during the most challenging task (RBOS) was associated with increases in COP sway velocity, COP variability and TA activation. Our results suggest that despite the potential energetic benefits from offloading the plantar flexors, passive ankle exoskeletons may induce unintended effects that hinder the control of standing balance, particularly during more challenging conditions. Further work is needed to determine the mechanisms underlying these effects.

records.title: A Focused Narrative Review of Selected Evidence on Gymnastics Training Optimization, Technology, Athlete Health, and Injury Prevention.
records.abstract: Background: Sustainable gymnastics training requires a balance between performance development, injury prevention, workload management, athlete health, psychological well-being, and long-term participation. This focused narrative review aimed to synthesize selected evidence on training optimization, technological applications, athlete health and injury prevention in gymnastics. Methods: A structured narrative review was conducted using the Web of Science Core Collection. The literature search covered publications issued between 1 January 2005 and 30 September 2025, with the final search performed on 30 September 2025. English-language publications retrieved through three predefined Topic searches in the Web of Science Core Collection were considered. The searches covered the period from 1 January 2005 to 30 September 2025 and were restricted to the Sport Sciences category. No additional publications were identified through reference-list screening. Three complementary thematic searches addressing gymnastics training models, technological applications, and injury prevention identified 485 records. After applying the eligibility criteria, removing duplicates, assessing full texts, and excluding ineligible or retracted publications, 140 publications were included in the narrative synthesis. No formal risk-of-bias assessment was performed. Results: The reviewed evidence emphasized progressive and individualized training, workload monitoring, recovery, physical preparation, age-appropriate development, and early identification of pain, fatigue, and other health-related concerns. Injury occurrence was associated with biomechanical loading, rapid growth, training exposure, previous injuries, insufficient recovery, menstrual dysfunction, psychological factors, and discipline-specific technical demands. Wearable sensors, video analysis, biomechanical modelling, artificial intelligence, virtual reality, and digital learning platforms supported movement assessment, technical feedback, training monitoring, and education. Evidence for several emerging technological applications, particularly artificial intelligence and automated assessment, remains preliminary and requires further validation in gymnastics-specific and real-world settings. However, substantial differences in study designs, populations, technologies, outcome measures, and methodological characteristics limited direct comparison across studies. Coaching communication, athlete motivation, psychological well-being, and access to validated technologies also influenced the sustainability of gymnastics training. Conclusions: Sustainable gymnastics training may benefit from an interdisciplinary and athlete-centered approach integrating individualized load management, injury prevention, health monitoring, recovery, educational coaching practices, and appropriately validated technologies. The evidence identified in this review highlights converging themes suggesting the potential value of combining these components to support safe performance development and long-term participation. However, more longitudinal, discipline-specific, and methodologically consistent research is needed.

records.title: A scoping review evaluating artificial intelligence applications across various injury prevention domains.
records.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly utilized for injury prevention across diverse clinical and community settings including machine learning (ML). This scoping review aimed to synthesize the current literature on the applications and predictive performance of AI across multiple injury prevention domains. This scoping review searched five major databases, including PubMed, Embase, ScienceDirect, ProQuest, and the Cochrane Library, to identify studies evaluating AI applications for injury prevention published through May 2026. Eligible studies included original U.S.-based, English-language research across self-harm and suicide, abuse and violence, fall prevention, and sports injury prediction. Studies were excluded if they lacked measurable prevention outcomes or sufficient methodological detail, or focused on injury treatment rather than prevention, to ensure relevant and interpretable evidence for synthesis. Nineteen studies met the inclusion criteria. ML models generally outperformed or matched traditional screening methods for self-harm and suicide prediction (AUC 0.81-0.82), while multimodal approaches achieved the highest predictive accuracy (AUC 0.90). In abuse and violence prevention, AI predicted intimate partner violence with an AUC of 0.88 and identified cases before formal disclosure. AI also improved fall risk assessment by accurately categorizing patient risk levels, predicting future falls, and mitigating fall injuries through wearable airbag technology. ML models predicted future sports-related injuries (AUC 0.76-0.84), while identifying modifiable risk factors including workload, strength deficits, prior injury burden, and concussion history. ML-based prediction showed promise for risk stratification in self-harm, suicide, intimate partner violence, and recurrent victimization. Additionally, AI predicted fall risk and identified athletes at risk for future sports-related injuries while detecting modifiable risk factors, including workload, prior injury burden, and strength deficits. Although these findings suggest that AI and ML may have potential applications in supporting earlier risk identification, informing targeted prevention strategies, and facilitating more personalized approaches to injury prevention, the limited available evidence warrants careful interpretation.

records.title: A Semi-Active Ankle Prosthesis With Automatic Transitions Between Passive and Active Modes.
records.abstract: The most commonly prescribed ankle/foot prostheses are energy storage and return (ESR) devices, which have good performance in level ground walking, but have limited functionality in tasks requiring ankle mobility, such as stair ascent or descent. Powered prostheses aim to address this limitation by actively controlling the joint with actuators, but they tend to be heavier and taller and become unusable when the battery is depleted, hindering their clinical adoption. In this paper, we present a semi-active ankle prosthesis that integrates the energy storage and return characteristics of a passive prosthesis with the active joint articulation of a powered prosthesis. The proposed prosthesis combines a novel brake mechanism with a series elastic actuator to enable Passive and Active operation modes within a compact build height (141 mm) and lightweight (1.4 kg without batteries) form factor. Experimental validation with one lower-limb amputee demonstrates that the proposed prosthesis reproduces the gait dynamics of a passive prosthesis, independent of battery charge, in Passive mode, and matches the range of motion and actuation capabilities of a powered device during stair ascent and sit-to-stand transitions in Active mode. Automatic transitions between modes within a gait cycle allow for incline adaptation. Moreover, automatic transitions between gait cycles allow for seamless transitions between passive walking and active stair ambulation. This combination of functionalities has never been demonstrated in an ankle prosthesis and has the potential to improve mobility among the amputee population.

records.title: Ankle Foot Orthosis Intervention Improves the Ground Reaction Forces During Walking in Patients with Peripheral Artery Disease (Randomized Clinical Trial).
records.abstract: This study investigated the impact of walking with ankle-foot-orthoses (AFOs) and without AFOs (non-AFO) on ground reaction forces (GRFs) in patients with peripheral artery disease (PAD). Additionally, this study examined the effect of AFO intervention vs. no AFO intervention on GRFs while walking with and without AFOs. Fifty patients with PAD were randomly assigned to either a three-month intervention (AFO) or a control (standard-of-care) group. After three months, subjects crossed over to the alternate group and were evaluated after three additional months. GRF data (anterior-posterior, medial-lateral, and vertical) were collected during walking with and without AFOs at baseline, three, and six months. Peak discrete GRF points, braking and propulsion impulses were compared across conditions, groups, and time points using linear mixed models. The peak brake and propulsion GRF were significantly reduced while walking with AFOs versus non-AFO (p < 0.01). Compared to non-AFO, walking with AFOs significantly reduced lateral GRF magnitude (p = 0.03) and significantly increased medial GRF (p = 0.02). The first and second maximum (p < 0.01) vertical GRF were significantly increased with AFOs versus non-AFOs. Walking with AFOs helped patients with PAD achieve greater peak propulsion and vertical GRFs compared to non-AFO, with GRF values trending toward those previously reported in healthy individuals.

records.title: Ankle Proprioceptive Performance on Increasingly Challenging Functional Tasks in Groups With and Without Chronic Ankle Instability.
records.abstract: Up to 75% of lateral ankle sprain cases experience long-term impairments and suffer chronic ankle instability (CAI), a condition characterized by impaired ankle proprioception. This study aims to investigate ankle proprioceptive performance during functional tasks with increasing movement control and ankle joint load in individuals with and without CAI. Cross-sectional study. Twenty individuals with CAI and 19 healthy controls completed 4 proprioceptive tasks: standing, walking, landing (double-leg drop), and stair descent. In each task, their ability to discriminate between 4 ankle inversion angles was assessed using a task-specific discrimination apparatus. CAI participants had significantly lower ankle proprioception scores than controls (mean difference = 0.047, 95% CI, 0.031-0.063). Proprioceptive acuity varied by task (P < .001, ηp2=.345), with no significant group-by-task interaction (P = .220, ηp2=.039). Trend analysis showed a linear improvement in proprioceptive performance with increasing ankle load and challenge in controls (P < .001, ηp2=.685), whereas the CAI group showed both significant linear (P < .001, ηp2=.445) and quadratic (P = .001, ηp2=.430) trends, reflecting a rise followed by a significant downturn as load peaked. Both groups improved with greater load, but during stair descent, individuals with CAI exhibited a significant decline. This suggests that proprioceptive processing in CAI is impaired and may be overloaded during highly challenging tasks.

records.title: Association of Ankle Joint Moment and Ankle Joint Velocity With 60° Ipsilateral Change-of-Direction Performance.
records.abstract: Chen, C-H, Yeh, M-C, Liu, C, Tseng, Y-J, and Lu, S-T. Association of ankle joint moment and ankle joint velocity with 60° ipsilateral change-of-direction performance. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The rapid acceleration and deceleration associated with a change of direction (COD) is associated with high ankle loading, including high ankle moment and velocity, which have been linked to ankle sprain or chronic ankle instability. Although the correlations between ankle joint loading and contralateral COD (contra-COD) have been investigated, one study reported that ipsilateral COD (ipsi-COD) and contra-COD involve distinct, asymmetrical mechanisms. Therefore, the aim of this study is to evaluate the associations of ankle joint moment and ankle joint velocity with 60° ipsi-COD performance. Thirty-five male athletes of recreational team sports performed an ipsi-COD task with their nondominant leg. A three-dimensional motion-capture system and a force platform were used to collect biomechanical data. Ground contact time was negatively associated with plantarflexion moment ( r = -0.511) and inversion moment ( r = -0.424). By contrast, horizontal impulse was positively correlated with plantarflexion moment ( r = 0.407). No correlation was observed between ground contact time and ground reaction force. The moderate negative correlations of ground contact time with plantarflexion moment and inversion moment suggest that increasing ipsi-COD performance may result in high ankle moments and potentially excessive ankle loading. In addition, the absence of a correlation between ground contact time and GRF suggests that athletes consider focusing on converting their approaching velocity to the intended direction during ipsi-COD, as this study indicates that ground reaction force and impulse are not associated with ipsi-COD performance.

records.title: Audit of Surgical Complications Post-limb Salvage Procedures for Aggressive Bone Tumours at a Developing Tumour Unit.
records.abstract: Background The incidence of malignant bone tumours remains relatively low in our setting. However, our patients typically present late with large tumour volumes, making limb-salvage procedures difficult and prone to post-operative complications. Due to a paucity of literature in a clinical context similar to ours, we elected to assess complications experienced by our cohort of patients.  Aim & setting We aimed to study complications experienced by our patient cohort post-limb salvage and tumour prosthesis replacement for aggressive bone tumours. This study was set at the Chris Hani Baragwanath Academic Hospital Teaching Hospital in Johannesburg from January 2017 to December 2024. Methods We conducted a retrospective review of records of patients who underwent limb salvage for aggressive musculoskeletal tumours at our hospital. Patients with aggressive bone tumours treated at a different unit and those who underwent revision surgery were excluded from the study. Demographic data, pathology factors, and surgery factors were extracted for analysis. Descriptive statistics were computed using Stata 18 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, Texas). Results A total of 20 patient records met the inclusion criteria for review. The majority of the patients were of African descent, with all age groups having an equal distribution of the burden of disease: five (0-17 years), five (18-24 years), five (25-34 years), and five (> 35 years). Osteosarcoma accounted for 45% (9/20) of diagnoses, followed by giant cell tumour (GCT) of bone. Our cohort showed a significant predilection for lower-limb involvement, with the latter accounting for 90%(18/20) of cases. Seventy percent of our patients experienced complications, with a majority of complications being prosthesis-related, such as prosthetic joint infection (PJIs) and instability.  Conclusion The use of limb-salvage surgery with tumour prosthesis implants for malignant bone tumours is a significant achievement in bone tumour care; however, not without complications. Neurovascular injury, muscle weakness and PJIs have a predilection for the lower limb, while prosthetic instability is likely following proximal humerus resection and replacement joint. Early presentation and meticulous soft-tissue preservation could reduce our complication rate. Contribution The findings highlight our experience treating aggressive bone tumours with limb-salvage surgery in our clinical context.

records.title: Auditory Biofeedback Gait Training in Individuals With Chronic Ankle Instability: Protocol for a Randomized Controlled Trial.
records.abstract: Chronic ankle instability (CAI) develops in a large majority of patients with lateral ankle sprain (LAS), who often experience recurring injuries, residual feelings of instability, and abnormal neuromuscular patterns. Specifically, gait alterations are common in those with CAI and considered a contributing factor to poor long-term ankle joint health. Yet, there are no evidence-based gait-training protocols targeted to improve biomechanics, which may improve long-term outcomes related to ankle joint health and patient satisfaction. This study protocol introduces a progressive auditory biofeedback (ABF) gait-training program aimed to improve short- and long-term lower extremity biomechanics and talar cartilage outcomes and reduce the frequency of ankle-giving-way episodes and recurring injuries. This study is a multisite randomized controlled trial (RCT) with a target enrollment of 100 patients with CAI into a control group (n=50, 50%) or an ABF gait-training program (n=50, 50%). Both groups will complete a progressive 6-week (12-session) protocol comprising walking, ruck marching, and running on a treadmill. Lower extremity kinematics and kinetics, talar cartilage characteristics (via ultrasonography), self-perceived dysfunction and instability, and number of recurring sprains will be assessed prior to intervention, immediately after intervention, and 6 and 12 months postintervention. Finally, the frequency of ankle-giving-way episodes in the 6 months prior to intervention will be compared to the frequency of episodes at the 6- and 12-month time points to determine a longitudinal difference in ankle-giving-way episodes. The study was funded in September 2024 and prospectively registered through ClinicalTrials.gov on March 10, 2025. The first participant was enrolled in May 2025. As of August 2026, 118 individuals had been recruited and 19 participants enrolled. Recruitment will remain open until September 2027, and study completion is expected in September 2028. Data processing is projected to continue through September 2028, with the final report published in June 2029. This study will be the first RCT of ABF gait training to assess the immediate and long-term effects on lower extremity biomechanics, ankle joint health, and patient-reported outcomes in patients with CAI. Results from this study will advance the knowledge of long-term joint health that may be associated with poor outcomes post-LAS. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06868316; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06868316. DERR1-10.2196/107775.

records.title: Autologous Osteochondral Transplantation Remains a Reliable Option for Talar Osteochondral Lesions, With Low Knee Donor-Site Morbidity.
records.abstract: Autologous osteochondral transplantation (AOT) is a surgical option for talar osteochondral lesions (OCL), with favorable outcomes and high return-to-sport rates; however, knee donor-site morbidity remains a concern. To evaluate clinical and functional outcomes, complications, return to work and sport, and satisfaction after AOT for talar OCL. Retrospective case series. We retrospectively reviewed consecutive patients ≥18 years with talar OCL treated with AOT (2011-2022; minimum 2-year follow-up); patients with prior knee pain or surgery, infection, advanced osteoarthritis, or rheumatologic disease were excluded. Outcomes included the AOFAS hindfoot, Lysholm, and Tegner scores, ankle and knee visual analog scale (VAS) pain, satisfaction, return to work and sport, and complications. Thirty-seven patients (78% male; median age, 36 years; median follow-up, 24 months) were included. Median lesion size was 150 mm², all medial; 14 (38%) had concomitant procedures. The AOFAS score improved from 54.5 to 95.8 (mean difference, 41.3; 95% CI, 38.4-44.3) and ankle VAS from 7.0 to 1.6 (-5.4; 95% CI, -5.9 to -4.9) (both p < 0.001). Postoperative Lysholm score was 98.8 ± 4.0 and knee VAS 1.2 ± 0.8 (no preoperative knee scores). Return to work took 2.3 ± 1.2 months; all 32 athletes resumed sport at 6.5 ± 2.1 months, 20 (63%) in their pre-injury sport. Tegner scores were unchanged (5.4 vs 5.5; p = 0.624). One knee hemarthrosis and one repeat ankle arthroscopy occurred. AOT for talar OCL yielded favorable short-term outcomes, high return-to-work and return-to-sport rates, and low reported knee donor-site morbidity; baseline knee scores were unavailable. 4.

records.title: Beyond the Sagittal Plane: The Lateral Countermovement Jump as a Clinical Tool for Return-to-Play Decision-Making and Performance Evaluation.
records.abstract: Return-to-play (RTP) decision-making after lower-extremity injury has traditionally emphasized sagittal-plane assessments, including double and single leg vertical jump metrics, double and single-leg hop batteries, and quadriceps strength limb symmetry indices (LSI). Yet many sports place a disproportionate demand on frontal-plane, lateral force production; basketball players, for example, spend up to a third of their live game actions in a defensive shuffle or lateral cutting posture. Recent force-plate evidence supports the single-leg lateral countermovement jump (LCMJ) as a reliable, time-efficient, and low-load assessment capable of stratifying lateral movement competency in elite athletes. This clinical commentary reviews recent reliability and discriminant-validity data on the LCMJ, places the test within the broader RTP evidence base and its known limitations, and proposes a practical framework for incorporating relative lateral force testing into RTP and performance batteries used by physical therapists and sports medicine clinicians.

records.title: Biomechanical and movement-quality predictors of lower-limb load-related injury in collegiate athletes: a prospective cohort study using functional movement screening, wearable inertial sensing, and explainable machine learning.
records.abstract: Lower-limb load-related injuries account for a disproportionate share of time loss in collegiate sport, yet the biomechanical and movement-quality factors distinguishing injured from uninjured athletes remain incompletely characterized. This prospective cohort study followed 161 collegiate athletes for one competitive season, integrating Functional Movement Screen task-level scores with wearable inertial measurement unit-derived features - including peak tibial acceleration asymmetry, surrogate vertical loading rate, and pelvis-trunk stability indices - within an explainable machine learning framework. Four classifiers were compared across FMS-only, wearable-only, and fused configurations under nested five-fold cross-validation with embedded LASSO feature selection. Thirty-seven load-related time-loss injuries were recorded (23.0% incidence). The fused XGBoost model achieved an out-of-fold AUC of 0.70 (95% CI: 0.61-0.79), outperforming FMS-only (AUC 0.62) and wearable-only (AUC 0.64) configurations by statistically significant margins. Peak tibial acceleration asymmetry and surrogate loading rate on the non-dominant limb were the strongest biomechanical predictors; in-line lunge and active straight-leg raise task scores contributed most among FMS inputs. Biomechanical features added an independent AUC increment of 0.07 beyond previous-injury history. SHAP analysis identified an interaction between tibial impact asymmetry and in-line lunge score that met the pre-specified directional stability criterion. These findings establish a physiologically interpretable template for biomechanical phenotyping of injury risk, supporting the combined use of wearable sensing and task-level movement screening in collegiate athletic populations.

records.title: Building smarter surveillance: a framework for artificial intelligence-enabled monitoring of overuse injuries in youth sports.
records.abstract: Early sport specialization (ESS), defined as intensive, year-round training in a single sport at the exclusion of others, has become increasingly prevalent among youth athletes. This trend has coincided with a rise in overuse injuries, and premature attrition. Concurrently, advances in wearable sensors and artificial intelligence (AI) enable real-time quantification of training load, biomechanical deviations, and recovery. However, a translational gap remains: existing AI surveillance models are predominantly validated in elite adult male cohorts, leaving youth athletes underserved. To address this gap, we propose a translational four-pillar framework for ESS-aware AI injury monitoring in youth sport. Bridging technological capabilities with developmental physiology through structured AI surveillance provides a structured risk-monitoring roadmap with the potential to inform preventative strategies, optimize physical readiness, and support long-term musculoskeletal health in youth athletes.

records.title: Calf Injuries: Anatomy, Pathology, and Treatment.
records.abstract: Calf injuries are common in athletes and typically result in missed time from sport and activities of daily living. The three individual triceps surae muscles can be injured, with differing described mechanisms. Gastrocnemius or plantaris strains tend to occur during sudden explosive movement of the ankle from a dorsiflexed to a plantarflexed position with the knee in extension. Soleus strains typically occur from repetitive dorsiflexion of the ankle with the knee flexed. Imaging modalities such as magnetic resonance imaging and ultrasonography can be helpful in determining the location and grade of injury, which can aid in treatment and return to play timelines. Classically, these injuries have been graded as grade I, II, or III, with grade I having <10% muscle fiber disruption, grade II having >10 to 50% muscle fiber disruption, and grade III having 50 to 100% muscle fiber disruption. The mainstay of treatment for most calf strains is nonsurgical, with surgical management being rare but reported in the literature for isolated grade III ruptures of the medial head of the gastrocnemius. Return to sport and activities requires a graduated physical therapy program focused on restoring tissue length without excessive strain. Recent limited evidence has shown promising results with quicker return to activities and decreased pain with platelet-rich plasma injections.

records.title: Clinical Decision Rules and Reduction of Ankle X-Rays in Pediatric Population: An Intervention Study.
records.abstract: Ankle injuries are common in pediatric patients and have a low incidence of fractures. This study aimed to evaluate the implementation of a protocol based on clinical decision rules to reduce the number of radiographs requested during nursing triage, thereby decreasing radiation exposure, waiting times, and health care costs. A quasi-experimental pre- and postintervention study with nonequivalent groups was conducted. Patients aged 3 to 16 years presenting with ankle injuries to the emergency department were included. The number of radiographs requested before and after the protocol's implementation was compared. The protocol incorporated the Ottawa Ankle Rules and the Low-Risk Ankle Rule, which were applied during nursing triage and medical assessment. The absolute risk reduction, relative risk reduction, and number needed to treat were calculated, along with the emergency department length of stay and associated economic savings. A total of 252 patients were included (preintervention: 132 and postintervention: 120). Radiograph requests decreased significantly, with an absolute risk reduction of 46.81% (95% CI, 36.59%-57.03%), a relative risk reduction of 51.93% (95% CI, 40.57%-61.12%), and a number needed to treat of 2 (95% CI, 1-2). Interobserver agreement between nursing staff and physicians was good to very good (Cohen's kappa of 0.779 for Ottawa Ankle Rules and 0.825 for Low-Risk Ankle Rule). The implementation of clinical decision rules by nursing staff significantly reduces radiograph requests in pediatric ankle injuries without compromising safety. This strategy reduces radiation exposure, health care costs, and emergency department length of stay.

records.title: Comparative Effectiveness of Digital Exercise-Based Interventions for Improving Balance in Older Adults: Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis With GRADE Certainty of Evidence.
records.abstract: Technology-based rehabilitation is increasingly used for balance training in older adults. A 2023 network meta-analysis (NMA) found only exergaming with motion capture superior to no treatment; however, the evidence has since expanded, and no GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) appraisal has been applied. This study aimed to update the comparative effectiveness of 5 technology categories-exergaming with balance platforms (EBP), exergaming with motion capture (EMC), other serious games, interventions with wearables, and telerehabilitation (Tele)-versus conventional exercise (CE), and no treatment (NT), applying GRADE adapted for NMA. A systematic search of 4 databases from inception through April 2025, with an identical supplementary update search to January 31, 2026, identified 60 randomized controlled trials (N=3469; mean age 73.1, SD 5.2; range 63.3-86.2 y). Fifty-seven trials (2758 analyzed participants) contributed to 4 prespecified networks (all balance, functional scales, Timed Up and Go [TUG] test, and gait speed). A random-effects NMA was fitted using multivariate meta-regression. Treatment hierarchies were summarized by the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) and the probability of being best; certainty of evidence was rated with GRADE adapted for NMA. In the all-balance network, Tele (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.69, 95% CI 0.08-1.29; P=.03), EBP (SMD 0.63, 95% CI 0.31-0.95; P<.001), EMC (SMD 0.58, 95% CI 0.22-0.95; P=.002), and CE (SMD 0.35, 95% CI 0.03-0.68; P=.03) were superior to NT, with consistent findings in the TUG network (EBP 0.81, 95% CI 0.42-1.20; Tele 0.82, 95% CI 0.16-1.49; EMC 0.79, 95% CI 0.36-1.21; all P<.05). Tele ranked first by SUCRA (76.3%), but its probability of being best was only approximately 41%, and the estimate rested on 5 trials (n=198). No technology-based intervention was superior to CE in any network. Certainty of evidence was moderate for EBP versus NT and EMC versus NT in the TUG network only; the 37 other comparisons were low or very low. Dropout did not differ between technology-based and control arms (odds ratio 1.10, 95% CI 0.87-1.40; P=.41). Tele, EBP, and EMC were each associated with improved balance versus NT, although none exceeded CE. The first-place SUCRA ranking of Tele is preliminary. Certainty was moderate only for EBP and EMC versus NT on the TUG test; the remaining evidence is too uncertain for firm clinical recommendations. As no included trial reported falls, these findings are not direct evidence of fall prevention. Larger trials with standardized comparator intensity and posttraining follow-up are required.

records.title: Comparison of Different Coracoclavicular Stabilization Techniques in Acute Acromioclavicular Injury With Augmented Acromioclavicular Ligament Repair: A Whole-Body Cadaveric Study.
records.abstract: Acute acromioclavicular (AC) joint injuries account for approximately half of all shoulder injuries in sports trauma, and the optimal surgical strategy remains controversial. Contemporary surgical management increasingly combines coracoclavicular (CC) stabilization with augmented AC ligament repair. However, the relative kinematic performance of different CC stabilization techniques in the presence of AC repair has not been previously investigated. To compare 3 CC stabilization techniques-coracoclavicular loop, single clavicular tunnel, and double clavicular tunnel-each combined with double-row AC ligament repair, to determine which technique most closely restores physiologic scapular and clavicular motion. Controlled laboratory study. Eight shoulders from 4 fresh-frozen whole-body cadavers were assessed. Each shoulder was passively taken through forward flexion, abduction, and horizontal adduction by a single operator at a standardized cadence, while 3-dimensional scapular and clavicular motions were recorded using an inertial measurement unit-based system. Kinematics were evaluated under intact conditions, after sequential ligament transections, and following each reconstruction technique, analyzed using mixed-effects models and polynomial regression. Significant kinematic deviations were observed following AC and CC ligament transection, particularly beyond 120° of elevation. None of the techniques fully restored native motion. The double-tunnel construct showed the smallest deviation from intact scapular external rotation, while all 3 repair techniques produced similar reductions in clavicular motion. The single-tunnel construct showed the greatest deviation, while the loop technique produced intermediate results. All reconstructions showed persistent scapular rotation increases and reduced clavicular dynamics at higher elevation angles. When combined with AC ligament repair, the double-tunnel CC stabilization most closely approximated physiologic scapular and clavicular motion. However, kinematic deviations beyond 120° of arm elevation suggest a zone of mechanical vulnerability across all techniques. Among the 3 CC stabilization techniques tested with concurrent AC ligament repair, the double-tunnel construct most closely restored physiologic scapular and clavicular motion and may be considered the preferred technique. Surgeons may consider restricting arm elevation to <120° during early rehabilitation, as kinematic deviations beyond this range may reflect patterns consistent with scapular dyskinesis.

records.title: Comparison of Soccer-Related Injuries at US Emergency Departments Between High School-Aged and College-Aged Athletes: A 10-Year NEISS Analysis, 2015-2024.
records.abstract: Soccer is widely played in the United States (US), yet contemporary national data comparing soccer-related emergency department (ED) injuries between high school-aged and college-aged athletes remain limited. To provide a comparative assessment of soccer-related injuries among high school-aged and college-aged athletes and to characterize the burden of these injuries on US EDs. Descriptive epidemiological study. The National Electronic Injury Surveillance System was queried for soccer-related injuries among patients aged 14 to 23 years from 2015 to 2024. Patients aged 14 to 18 years were categorized as high school-aged and those aged 19 to 23 years as college-aged. Weighted national estimates were calculated using National Electronic Injury Surveillance System (NEISS) sampling weights. Participation denominators were derived from National Federation of State High School Associations boys' and girls' soccer participation for the high school-aged group and National Collegiate Athletic Association men's and women's soccer participation across Divisions I, II, and III for the college-aged group. Incidence rates were expressed per 100 participants, and incidence rate ratios (IRRs) with 95% CIs were calculated. A total of 29,144 NEISS cases corresponded to a weighted national estimate of 877,548 soccer-related injuries treated in US EDs. High school-aged athletes accounted for 687,302 injuries, whereas college-aged athletes accounted for 190,246. The incidence rate was 8.19 per 100 participants among high school-aged athletes and 34.73 among college-aged athletes (IRR, 4.24; 95% CI, 4.22-4.26), indicating an approximately 4-fold higher per-participant rate among college-aged athletes. Per-participant rates were higher in the college-aged group in every study year and across all body region, diagnosis, and disposition categories. The ankle (157,321 injuries; 17.9%), knee (137,030; 15.6%), head (127,695; 14.6%), and wrist (52,940; 6%) were the most frequently injured body regions; strains and sprains were the most common diagnosis (262,189; 29.9%). Most injuries were treated and discharged (96.8%), whereas transfers or admissions were uncommon (1.9%). College-aged athletes had over a 4-fold higher rate of soccer-related ED injury than high school-aged athletes, despite high school-aged athletes accounting for most total ED visits. These findings highlight important differences between absolute ED burden and participation-indexed injury rates. They may help inform injury-prevention priorities, ED counseling, and postinjury follow-up strategies across scholastic and collegiate soccer populations.

records.title: Conductive Composite-Based Wearable Sensors for Sports Science: Intelligent Data Analysis and Emerging Applications.
records.abstract: Wearable sensors enable continuous acquisition of physiological, biochemical, and biomechanical signals during exercise, providing data to support sports performance assessment, training regulation, fatigue monitoring, and rehabilitation interventions. However, signal reliability and multidimensional data analysis under complex motion conditions remain constrained by device functionality. Conductive composites can improve sensor flexibility, interfacial conformability, and signal acquisition performance, while artificial intelligence (AI) enables movement pattern recognition, state assessment, and outcome prediction from complex data. Their integration is advancing wearable systems toward multimodal sensing and intelligent analysis. Guided by application needs in sports, this review summarizes emerging applications of wearable sensing technologies enabled by conductive composites and AI. First, the relevance to sports science and the data characteristics of physiological, biochemical, and biomechanical signals are introduced. The functional characteristics, representative applications, and major limitations of conductive polymer, carbon-based, MXene, and hydrogel composites are then summarized. Regarding algorithms, the fundamental principles of supervised learning, unsupervised learning, deep learning (DL), and large language models (LLMs) are discussed, with comparisons of their capabilities in feature extraction, temporal modeling, and multisource data analysis, as well as their input data requirements. On this basis, advances in the application of these systems to sports performance and sport-specific movement monitoring, exercise-induced fatigue monitoring and assessment, sports injury identification and evaluation, and intelligent monitoring of sports rehabilitation are reviewed followed by a discussion of current challenges and future directions. Through the coordinated integration of material design, signal acquisition, and intelligent analysis, wearable systems are expected to enable continuous, reliable, and individualized assessment of exercise-related states, with further applications in real-time feedback, risk alerts, and training decision support, providing a technological foundation for scientifically informed training, sports rehabilitation, and individual health management.

records.title: Consumer Grade Wearable Sensor Metrics Are Associated with Internal Forces at Common Running Injury Locations.
records.abstract: Inexpensive consumer-grade wearable sensors have expanded possibilities to assess, monitor, or modify a runner's gait. However, it is unclear which sensor-measured gait metrics are strongly associated with internal loading at common injury locations. To measure the association between gait metrics measured by consumer-grade wearable sensors and internal forces at the Achilles tendon and the patellofemoral joint. 55 healthy runners wearing consumer-grade chest straps foot-pods completed a 38-minute run on an instrumented treadmill at 12 speeds from 70%-125% of self-reported typical running pace. A scaled musculoskeletal model derived from motion capture data and driven by static optimization was used to calculate Achilles tendon and patellofemoral joint forces during stance for each speed. Functional regression models were used to estimate the associations of each of nine sensor-measured gait metrics with internal forces across stance, after adjusting for body mass and running speed. At both the Achilles tendon and the patellofemoral joint, cadence, vertical oscillation, and vertical ratio (vertical oscillation divided by step length) showed the strongest associations with internal forces (maximum of 0.4-0.6 BW change in force per one standard deviation change in the gait metric). Other wearable sensor-measured gait metrics, including stance time, leg stiffness, and stance time percent showed weaker associations (<0.4 BW change in force per one standard deviation change in the gait metric). Runners with higher-than-average cadence, vertical oscillation, or vertical ratio values experience marked differences in internal forces at the Achilles tendon and patellofemoral joint. Of these gait metrics, cadence is the most practical for out-of-lab use because of its ease of accurate measurement with consumer-grade devices.

records.title: Cost Analysis and Clinical Outcomes of Staged Versus Single-Stage Fixation in the Management of Trimalleolar Ankle Fractures.
records.abstract: Trimalleolar ankle fractures (TMFs) compromise ankle biomechanics; optimal operative strategy is debated. We compared single-stage open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) with staged external fixation (EF) plus ORIF for outcomes and hospital billed charges. Retrospective cohort of adults treated 2018-2022 at a tertiary center. EF + ORIF (n = 40) vs. ORIF (n = 49). length of stay (LOS), hospital billed charges (stage-1, stage-2, total), readmission, additional surgical procedures, complications, and visual analog scale (VAS), American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society (AOFAS), Short Form-36 (SF-36) to 2 years. After multivariable adjustment, ORIF was associated with a lower first-stage hospital billed charge (charge ratio, 0.55; 95% CI, 0.37-0.81; p = 0.003), a lower total hospital billed charge (charge ratio, 0.33; 95% CI, 0.24-0.47; p < 0.001), and earlier partial and full weight-bearing. Adjusted AOFAS scores were higher in the ORIF group at 3 months, 6 months, and 1 year, but not at 2 years. Holm-adjusted postoperative VAS contrasts were not significant, and the SF-36 group-by-time interaction was not significant. In this clinically selected cohort, single-stage ORIF was associated with lower hospital billed charges, earlier partial and full weight-bearing, and higher adjusted AOFAS scores at selected early follow-up points. Because Tscherne grade 2 and 3 injuries occurred only in the staged-treatment group, these findings do not establish comparative effectiveness for those injury grades or long-term functional superiority. Temporary external fixation remains an appropriate bridging strategy when soft-tissue conditions preclude immediate ORIF. Level III, retrospective cohort.

records.title: Cryotherapy added to PEACE & LOVE rehabilitation for acute lateral ankle sprain in physically active adults: A randomized controlled trial in sports rehabilitation.
records.abstract: To evaluate whether adding cryotherapy during the first 72 h to a standardized PEACE & LOVE rehabilitation program improves early recovery after acute lateral ankle sprain compared with a room-temperature gel-pack control. Randomized, parallel-group controlled trial. Sixty physically active adults with Grade I-II acute lateral ankle sprain within 48 h of injury were randomized 1:1 to PEACE & LOVE rehabilitation plus either active cryotherapy or room-temperature gel-pack control. Cryotherapy was delivered using a 0-4 °C gel pack for 20 min, three times daily for 72 h. Both groups received identical progressive rehabilitation for four weeks. The primary outcome was average ankle pain during the previous 24 h measured using the Numeric Pain Rating Scale at Day 7. Secondary outcomes were swelling, Lower Extremity Functional Scale score, Weight-Bearing Lunge Test, paracetamol use, and re-injury. Outcomes were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. All randomized participants completed follow-up. Pain decreased in both groups, with a statistically greater Day 7 reduction in cryotherapy than control (adjusted difference -1.10, 95% confidence interval -1.85 to -0.35; p = 0.004). However, this did not reach the pre-specified 2-point minimal clinically important difference. Swelling also decreased more with cryotherapy (-1.78 cm, 95% confidence interval -3.26 to -0.30; p = 0.019). Functional recovery, dorsiflexion, paracetamol use, and re-injury were comparable. Responder analysis produced a number needed to treat estimate with confidence intervals crossing infinity. Cryotherapy provided statistically greater short-term pain and swelling reductions, but its added clinical value beyond progressive rehabilitation remains uncertain within four weeks.

records.title: Design and Bench Evaluation of a Sensor-Integrated Prosthetic-Leg Prototype.
records.abstract: This study presents the design and preliminary bench evaluation of a sensor-integrated prosthetic-leg prototype. The platform combines a multi-material PAHT-CF/TPU 95A foot, articulated knee and ankle mechanisms, two surface electromyography channels, an MPU6050 inertial measurement unit, an Arduino Uno controller, and MG995 servomotors. EMG threshold crossings select discrete knee-servomotor commands, while an accelerometer-derived inclination estimate selects between two ankle-servomotor commands. The evaluation comprised exploratory finite-element analyses, separate static compression tests, and qualitative demonstrations of the sensor-to-actuator pathways. The foot model predicted a maximum displacement of 25.96 mm under 400 N, whereas a separate compression test recorded approximately 7 mm at 1000 N; these values do not constitute quantitative model validation because the loading, constraints, and displacement measures differed. The shank model produced a maximum equivalent stress of 23.89 MPa, and a separate shank-knee assembly test reached approximately 1.85 kN. The foot-ankle connection produced a stress estimate of 203.6 MPa against an assumed strength value of 60 MPa, identifying a critical design limitation. Functional observations demonstrated sensor-triggered command execution, but joint tracking accuracy, response time, actuator output under load, and control repeatability were not quantified. The prototype therefore provides an initial laboratory platform for investigating mechanical and sensing integration; structural redesign and quantitative bench testing are required before any load-bearing or clinical use can be considered.

records.title: Diagnostic Musculoskeletal Ultrasound in the Evaluation of the Extensor Digitorum Longus.
records.abstract: The extensor digitorum longus muscle and tendons are among the longer muscle-tendon units in the lower leg and foot. This feather-like, unipennate muscle is part of the anterior ankle group, attaching proximally along the lateral side of the lateral condyle of the tibia and the upper three-quarters of the fibula's inner surface. Near the ankle, the tendon narrows as it passes beneath the extensor retinacula and divides into four smaller tendons that connect to the toes. Since it crosses the ankle joint and attaches to the second through fifth toes, it facilitates dorsiflexion of the foot and extension of the toe joints. An accurate diagnosis of extensor digitorum longus tendonitis or rupture is crucial for appropriate treatment planning and optimal patient outcomes. Diagnostic musculoskeletal ultrasound (MSKUS) has become a widely used imaging modality for assessing many ankle and foot pathologies. It offers a portable, real-time, and cost-effective alternative that is gaining traction in rehabilitation and sports medicine settings. MSKUS has emerged as a valuable, non-invasive imaging modality for evaluating ankle and foot injuries. This manuscript reviews the utility of MSKUS in evaluating the quality, size, sonographic techniques, and clinical implications for rehabilitation professionals who need to visualize the extensor digitorum longus. By integrating MSKUS into clinical practice, providers can improve diagnostic accuracy, increase diagnostic confidence, monitor healing progression, and guide rehabilitation strategies to optimize outcomes for patients with ankle and foot injuries.

records.title: Double-level osteotomy versus high tibial osteotomy for varus malalignment of the knee: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
records.abstract: To compare double-level osteotomy (DLO) with high tibial osteotomy (HTO) for varus knee malalignment across patient-reported, radiographic, operative and complication outcomes. PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science were searched to 15 May 2026 for comparative DLO versus HTO studies. Outcomes were pooled with a random-effects model as mean differences (MD) or risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI), with absolute values for each arm. The primary outcome was joint-line obliquity (JLO). Sensitivity analyses (leave-one-out, one cohort per centre, comparable indications) were post hoc. Nine observational studies (805 knees; 306 DLO, 499 HTO) were included. At a mean follow-up of 3 years, postoperative JLO was lower after DLO than after HTO (four studies; 1.6° vs. 5.9°; MD: -4.14°, 95%CI: -5.22, -3.06; I2 = 76%). DLO produced a lower MPTA (seven studies; 91.3° vs. 95.4°; MD: -4.10°, 95%CI: -5.30, -2.90), LDFA (four studies; 86.0° vs. 90.2°; MD: -4.04°, 95%CI: -4.49, -3.58) and mLDFA (two studies; 85.6° vs. 89.0°; MD: -3.37°, 95%CI: -4.16, -2.58). The hip-knee-ankle angle difference was small (five studies; MD: -0.96°, 95%CI: -1.83, -0.09) and not robust in sensitivity analyses. No difference was demonstrated for joint-line convergence angle, posterior tibial slope, any KOOS subscale, KSS scores or time to return to sport. Operative time was longer with DLO (two studies; 137 vs. 91 min; MD: 42.9, 95%CI: 25.7, 60.2). Intraoperative hinge fracture was less frequent with DLO (three studies; 14.0% vs. 34.6%; RR: 0.41, 95%CI: 0.23, 0.73). No nonunion was reported. At 3 years, no significant difference in patient-reported or functional outcomes was demonstrated between DLO and HTO. DLO achieved correction with less JLO and fewer hinge fractures, at the cost of a longer operation. Because DLO was often selected for bifocal or larger deformities, the radiographic differences partly reflect the indication. These hypothesis-generating findings require prospective confirmation. Level I.

records.title: Dynamical systems-based metrics reveal fatigue-related biomechanical changes during running in endurance-trained male and female runners.
records.abstract: Linear and nonlinear metrics derived from a small number of accelerometers provide global insight into fatigue-related changes and injury risk. This study aimed to determine the effects of fatigue on movement dynamics estimated from lower-back accelerometry between endurance-trained male and female runners. Thirty-two endurance-trained runners (16 females) performed a fatiguing running task until volitional exhaustion (20 on the Borg CR20 scale), while wearing one inertial measurement unit (IMU) placed on their pelvis/lower back. Step and stride regularity (unbiased autocorrelation), root mean square (RMS)-based measures of variability (absolute RMS and RMS ratio), complexity (Sample Entropy), jerk-based measure of smoothness (Log Dimensionless Jerk; LDLJ), and stability (short- and long-term Lyapunov Exponent) were calculated from the raw accelerations. Significant main effects of fatigue were observed across both sexes for gait regularity, with an 8% reduction in anteroposterior step regularity and an 11% reduction in stride regularity. Fatigue also altered variability characteristics, resulting in a 12% increase in mediolateral absolute RMS, a 13% increase in anteroposterior absolute RMS, a 2% decrease in vertical RMS ratio, a 6% increase in mediolateral RMS ratio, and an 8% increase in anteroposterior RMS ratio. Fatigue increased movement complexity, as evidenced by a 14% increase in vertical Sample Entropy and an 11% increase in anteroposterior Sample Entropy. In addition to these overall fatigue effects, RMS-based measure of variability showed sex-specific responses. Interaction effects showed that males exhibited a 4% increase in the vertical absolute RMS of lower-back acceleration with fatigue, whereas females did not. Both male and female endurance-trained runners may adopt a less regular and less predictable whole-body movement pattern with fatigue, while RMS-based variability showed sex-specific responses, with increased fatigue-related changes in males. These findings highlight the importance of considering both general and sex-specific adaptations when monitoring fatigue.

records.title: Editorial: Assessment and monitoring of human movement, volume II.
Effects of chronic ankle instability on ipsilateral knee cartilage degeneration in mouse model.
records.abstract: To explore the effects of chronic ankle instability (CAI) on ipsilateral knee cartilage degeneration and the coupling relationship between the two joints through mouse model. Thirty C57BL/6J mice were divided into the Sham group, the CAI group, and the destabilization of medial meniscus (DMM) group. They were respectively subjected to sham surgery, anterior talofibular ligament and calcaneofibular ligament transection, and medial meniscus resection. The degeneration of knee cartilage was evaluated through kinematic experiments, imaging examinations and histopathological analysis within 12 weeks post-operation. The kinematic experiments exhibited significantly increased passing time and number of slips for CAI group compared to DMM group and Sham group during crossing the balance beam; the step length and step width of CAI group were also larger. Imaging examination revealed obvious osteochondral defects and osteosclerosis of the femoral condyles both in CAI group and DMM group at 12 weeks post-operation. However, the DMM group was more severely affected than CAI group, as its bone mineral density and bone volume fraction were both higher than CAI group. Histopathological analysis exhibited thinner cartilage layer, less chondrocytes and more disordered collagen fibers in DMM group than CAI group at 6 and 12 weeks post-operation. The modified Mankin score and OARSI score of DMM group were also significantly higher than CAI group, while both groups were higher than Sham group. CAI can cause cartilage degeneration of ipsilateral knee joint in mouse model, there is a coupling relationship between ankle joint and knee joint.

records.title: Effects of sensorimotor training combined with short foot exercise on knee and ankle gait kinematics in individuals with flatfoot: A preliminary study.
records.abstract: Flatfoot, a common condition characterized by medial longitudinal arch collapse, alters foot and lower-limb mechanics. Sensorimotor training and short-foot exercises can improve postural stability and functional performance. However, their combined effects on gait kinematics remain unclear. This preliminary study evaluated the 6-week effects of combining these interventions on knee and ankle gait kinematics in individuals with flexible flatfeet. Thirty-two asymptomatic young adults with flexible flatfoot (14 males, 18 females; navicular drop ≥ 10 mm) were randomly assigned to an experimental group (sensorimotor training combined with short-foot exercises; n = 16) or a control group (sensorimotor training only; n = 16) using sealed opaque envelopes. Training was conducted 3 times per week for 6 weeks in a motion laboratory. Gait kinematics were assessed pre- and post-intervention using the VICON motion system. Outcomes included peak ankle inversion, eversion, dorsiflexion, and plantarflexion angles, knee internal and external rotation angles, and range of motion (ROM) in the sagittal, frontal, and transverse planes. Two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance was used for the analysis. The partial eta squared (ηp2) was reported as the effect size. Baseline demographics (age, sex, and body mass index) were similar between groups (P > .05). Significant group × time interactions were observed for gait variables. The experimental group showed a significant increase in peak ankle inversion (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.53-2.71; P = .004; ηp2 = 0.244) and a decrease in peak eversion (95% CI: 1.68-4.89; P = .002; ηp2 = 0.279). Peak knee internal rotation significantly decreased (95% CI: -9.92 to -2.82; P = .006; ηp2 = 0.228). Reductions were also observed in sagittal plane ankle ROM (95% CI: -4.88 to -0.68; P = .001; ηp2 = 0.317) and transverse plane knee ROM (95% CI: -7.75 to -4.01; P = .003; ηp2 = 0.254). No significant changes were found in ankle dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, knee external rotation, or frontal plane ankle ROM (P = .088, .126, .766, .136, respectively; ηp2 = 0.003-0.094). Combined sensorimotor and short-foot training more effectively improved gait kinematics than sensorimotor training alone, suggesting a promising non-surgical approach for managing flatfoot.

records.title: Effects of the FIFA 11 + neuromuscular warm-up program on Move2Perform injury risk classification in youth amateur soccer players: a randomized controlled trial.
records.abstract: Lower extremity injuries are a major concern in youth soccer, where multifactorial risk factors interact and isolated screening tools have demonstrated limited predictive accuracy. Neuromuscular warm-up programs such as the FIFA 11 + have shown efficacy in reducing injury incidence, yet limited evidence exists on their effect when combined with multifactorial risk-classification frameworks in amateur youth populations. The present study aimed to evaluate the effects of an eight-week FIFA 11 + neuromuscular warm-up program on injury risk profiles-classified by the Move2Perform algorithm-and on functional performance and injury incidence in youth amateur male soccer players. In this parallel-group, single-blinded randomized controlled trial, 44 male amateur soccer players aged 15-18 years competing in a regional amateur league were randomly allocated, using computer-generated block randomization, to an experimental group (n = 22) or a control group (n = 22). Injury risk was classified using the Move2Perform algorithm, which integrates demographic data, injury history, the Functional Movement Screen (FMS), and the Lower Quarter Y-Balance Test (YBT-LQ). Additional outcomes included jump performance and isometric quadriceps and hamstring strength. The experimental group performed the FIFA 11 + program three times per week for eight weeks under the supervision of a certified physiotherapist, while the control group continued their routine warm-up. Time-loss injuries were recorded prospectively during the eight-week period. A mixed-design ANOVA was used to assess Group × Time interactions. The experimental group showed significant improvements in YBT-LQ composite scores, FMS total scores, jump test performance, and quadriceps strength (p < 0.05), with significant Group × Time interactions favoring the FIFA 11 + group. Move2Perform risk classification shifted favorably in the experimental group: athletes initially categorized as Moderate Risk showed the most pronounced improvement, transitioning to Slight Risk, and three athletes initially classified as Substantial Risk moved to the Slight Risk category (descriptively notable, but not reaching statistical significance for this subgroup). The experimental group experienced significantly fewer time-loss injuries (n = 2) than the control group (n = 8) over the eight-week period (p = 0.009), with significantly lower incidences of ankle sprains (p = 0.038) and hamstring strains (p = 0.041). Athletes classified as high risk by the Move2Perform algorithm sustained approximately a threefold increase in injury occurrence compared with their lower-risk counterparts. An eight-week, supervised FIFA 11 + neuromuscular warm-up program produced favorable shifts in Move2Perform injury risk classification and reduced time-loss injury incidence in youth amateur soccer players. Combining multifactorial injury risk classification with structured neuromuscular warm-up appears to be a practical and effective strategy for reducing lower extremity injury risk in this population, supporting the integration of preseason group-based prevention with individualized corrective approaches. ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT07713004. Registered on 17 July 2026. Retrospectively registered.

records.title: Estrogen Receptor Expression Changes After Puberty in the Porcine Anterior Cruciate Ligament.
records.abstract: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries disproportionately affect female adolescent athletes, with hormonal influences implicated in this sex disparity. However, the relationship between pubertal hormonal changes and ACL gene and protein expression remains poorly understood. This study characterized hormone receptor expression and transcriptional profiles in the anteromedial (AM) and posterolateral (PL) bundles of female porcine ACLs before and after puberty. ACL bundles were collected from pre-pubescent (8 weeks) and post-pubescent (> 8 months) female Yorkshire cross-breed pigs (n = 6/group) and analyzed using gene expression profiling, western blotting, and immunofluorescence. Pre-pubescent ACLs exhibited greater expression of primary matrix genes (COL1A1, COL1A2, ELN, TNMD), suggesting active matrix synthesis, while post-pubescent ACLs showed elevated secondary matrix genes (COL3A1, LUM, COMP), indicating a homeostatic state. Notably, estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) gene and protein expression were significantly greater in post-pubescent ACLs, particularly in AM bundles, whereas G protein-coupled estrogen receptor (GPR30) expression was elevated pre-puberty. Both receptors were distributed homogeneously throughout the tissue. Histologically, post-pubescent ACLs demonstrated decreased cellularity and thicker fascicles compared to pre-pubescent tissues. These findings indicate that ACL sensitivity to estrogen varies across development, with increased ERα expression post-puberty potentially rendering the ligament more responsive to circulating estrogen. This work provides foundational evidence for age-dependent hormonal responsiveness in the ACL and motivates further investigation into how sex hormones influence ACL injury risk in adolescent females.

records.title: Exploring the Impact of Ovarian Hormones on Cortical Drive and Quadriceps Performance in Uninjured Female Athletes.
records.abstract: Ovarian hormones fluctuate across the menstrual cycle (MC) and differ between oral contraceptive (OC) users and naturally menstruating (NM) individuals. Hormones may affect cortical drive to peripheral muscles through excitatory effects of estradiol and inhibitory effects of progesterone on the central nervous system. The impact of hormones on cortical drive is poorly understood. This study aimed to (1) determine the effects of MC phase and OC use on cortical drive and quadriceps performance and (2) determine the relationship between ovarian hormones and these outcomes. We hypothesized that cortical drive will differ between MC phases in NM individuals but not in OC users. Cortical drive will be positively associated with circulating estradiol. Fourteen NM individuals and 11 OC users completed two time points (high hormone: NM mid-luteal, OC active pill and low hormone: NM early follicular, OC placebo). Hormone concentrations were quantified using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. Quadriceps performance (isometric peak torque [PTISOM] and rate of torque development) was measured using an isokinetic dynamometer. Corticospinal excitability and intracortical excitability (short-interval intracortical inhibition [SICI] and intracortical facilitation) were assessed using transcranial magnetic stimulation. Linear mixed-effect models were used to examine hormone status, phase, and interaction effects. Linear regression determined associations between hormones, cortical drive, and strength. There were no significant main effects or interactions for any cortical drive measure. There was a phase by hormone status interaction on the rate of torque development from 0 to 100 ms (RTD100), with a greater RTD100 at the high hormone phase than at the low hormone phase in the NM group but no difference between time points in the OC group. There was a main effect of phase on PTISOM, with a greater PTISOM at the low hormone phase regardless of hormone status. SICI was negatively associated with estradiol. RTD100 was positively associated with progesterone and moderated by hormone status. MC phase did not impact cortical drive but did impact quadriceps performance. There were between-phase differences in speed of contraction among NM individuals but not among OC users. A higher progesterone level was associated with faster speed of contraction, especially among NM participants. (1)Corticospinal and intracortical excitability did not differ by menstrual cycle (MC) phase or oral contraceptive (OC) use.(2)Quadriceps rate of torque development was associated with progesterone concentration and varied across the MC, suggesting hormone expression influenced the rate of torque development (RTD) (speed of contraction).(3)The influence of endogenous ovarian hormones on RTD (speed of contraction) differed between OC users and naturally menstruating individuals. II.
