records.title: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy in common tendinopathies.
records.abstract: Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) was initially used for urologic issues only. After Valchanou and Michailov started applying it in orthopedics in 1991, they focused on treatment of pseudarthrosis and delayed fracture healing. Some years later, shockwave therapy was also used for tendinopathies. Today, ESWT is the first-choice treatment for tendinopathies and is unsurpassed in terms of effectivity and side effects. This article discusses common regions of lower extremity tendinopathies (greater trochanter pain syndrome, quadriceps tendinopathy, patellar tendinopathy, Achilles tendinopathy) in a narrative review of the evidence-based literature and guidelines of leading shockwave societies such as the International Society for Medical Shockwave Treatment (ISMST) and the Deutschsprachige internationale Gesellschaft für Extrakorporale Stosswellentherapie (DIGEST). Additional case studies are also presented. Extracorporeal shockwave therapy shows excellent results in the evidence-based literature and in clinical application. No other conservative treatment option in orthopedics is described as intensively in the evidence-based literature as shockwave therapy. ESWT seems to be more effective when it is accompanied by an eccentric loading/physiotherapy program. Extracorporeal shockwave therapy enables tendon regeneration, long-term improvement, and faster return to sport, with predictable side effects and excellent tolerance.

records.title: Feedforward neuromuscular control and dynamic postural stability in people with chronic ankle instability during single-leg landing.
records.abstract: Individuals with chronic ankle instability(CAI) show deficits in neuromuscular control and postural stability. While feedback mechanisms are well-studied, feedforward mechanisms during dynamic tasks remains underexplored. This study compared feedforward neuromuscular control and dynamic postural stability among CAI, coper and healthy groups. Fifteen CAI(23.5 ± 2.9 years, 11 M/4F), fifteen coper(24.1 ± 3.4 years, 12 M/3F) and fifteen healthy participants(25.5 ± 3.5 years, 11 M/4F) performed single-leg drop landings from 30 cm. Total centre of pressure movement during 1-second and 3-second(TOTEX1s&TOTEX3s), mediolateral sway distance(DML), peak vertical GRF(peak vGRF) and root-mean-square of mediolateral GRF in the first 0.4 s(RMS_ML_0.4) were recorded via force plate. Surface electromyography recorded muscle activity 200 ms before landing among tibialis anterior(TA), peroneus longus(PL) and gastrocnemius lateralis(GL). Pre-activation timing was calculated using the Teager-Kaiser energy operator(TKEO). Statistical analysis involved one-way ANOVA(α = 0.05) and Tukey post-hoc testing. Compared to healthy participants, CAI individuals displayed earlier TA(270 ± 73 ms vs. 85 ± 53 ms, p < 0.001) and PL(260 ± 87 ms vs. 102 ± 62 ms, p < 0.001) pre-activations, alongside higher TA activity(76 ± 27% vs. 35 ± 19%, p < 0.001) but lower PL activity(38 ± 14% vs. 77 ± 23%, p < 0.001). Higher RMS_ML_0.4(6.7 ± 1.3%BW vs. 5.6 ± 1.0%BW, p = 0.037), DML(55.6 ± 15.7 mm vs. 39.5 ± 9.0 mm, p < 0.001) and peak vGRF(334 ± 44%BW vs. 286 ± 59%BW, p = 0.041)were observed as well. Coper showed earlier GL pre-activation(169 ± 57 ms vs. 108 ± 67 ms, p = 0.021), increased activity(155 ± 40% vs. 97 ± 29%, p < 0.001) and decreased DML(42.7 ± 7.0 mm vs. 55.6 ± 15.7 mm, p = 0.008) compared to CAI individuals. CAI exhibited postural control deficits and ineffective feedforward control, shown by lower PL activity despite early pre-activation. Rate of force production training is advised. Increased GL activation may serve as a compensatory response in copers after initial ankle sprain.

records.title: Feedforward Pre-Activation of Lateral Ankle Muscles Is Insufficient Against Excessive Ankle Inversion During Perturbation in Individuals With Chronic Ankle Instability.
records.abstract: This study aimed to compare ankle kinematics and muscle activation between individuals with and without chronic ankle instability (CAI), both prior to and following landing on an inversion trapdoor during walking, with a particular focus on the feedforward pre-activation of lateral ankle muscles and the consequent ankle kinematics post-perturbation. Forty participants were enrolled, including 20 with CAI and 20 age- and sex-matched non-CAI controls. They walked at their own pace on a custom-designed walking platform equipped with a trapdoor programmed to trigger a 24° inversion perturbation, simulating lateral ankle sprain conditions, across three unanticipated trials. Their lower limb muscle electromyography and ankle kinematics were synchronously collected 200 ms pre- and 200 ms post-perturbation. Continuous between-group data were compared by independent sample t-tests. CAI individuals showed higher pre-activation in the peroneus longus (-200.0 to -196.4 ms, mean diff: -11.38%, p = 0.049; -54.6 to -11.0 ms, mean diff: -10.60%, p = 0.011) and the lateral gastrocnemius (-200.0 to -175.4 ms, mean diff: -7.62%, p = 0.029) prior to perturbation, and lower activation in the peroneus longus at 72.1 to 98.0 ms (mean diff: 17.46%, p = 0.029) post-perturbation. They also showed greater ankle inversion in four clusters post-perturbation (0 to 111.0 ms, mean diff: -4.85°, p < 0.001; 117.0 to 128.0 ms, mean diff: -1.83°, p = 0.020; 142.0 to 145.0 ms, mean diff: -1.30°, p = 0.047; 154.0 to 165.0 ms, mean diff: -1.05°, p = 0.019). CAI individuals exhibit higher feedforward pre-activation in lateral ankle muscles, which may be insufficient against excessive ankle inversion after landing on a trapdoor during walking.

records.title: FIM Motorcycling sport-specific extension of the IOC consensus statement: methods for recording and reporting of epidemiological data on injury and illness in sport 2020.
records.abstract: In 2020, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) released a consensus statement recommending standardised methods for recording and reporting illness and injury in sport. A key component of this statement was the recognition that sport-specific extensions should be developed to provide more detailed recommendations tailored to individual sports and/or settings. In response, the Fédération Internationale de Motocyclisme (FIM) Medical Commission convened a 15-member panel-comprising clinicians across multiple specialities, a sports scientist and two FIM delegates-to develop a consensus statement specific to motorcycling sport injury and illness surveillance. The panel reviewed existing consensus literature relevant to sport injury/illness surveillance and conducted two rounds of voting based on the IOC framework using a Delphi methodology. They then voted on key sport-specific recommendations to form the motorcycling sport-specific extension. The final manuscript was approved unanimously by all panel members after two rounds of revision. Relative to the parent IOC statement, this extension: (1) reframes injury categorisation and contact mechanisms around the combined rider-and-machine nature of motorcycling incidents; (2) replaces symptom-based and pathology-based severity scoring with a time-loss model adapted to the sport's irregular competition calendar, including explicit handling of estimated severity and right-censored cases; (3) restricts exposure measurement to motorcycle-mounted transponder data rather than wearable devices, for safety and regulatory reasons and (4) introduces a discipline-specific appendix covering fall/injury mechanisms, demographic and equipment-damage variables and primary/secondary exposure and severity measures across circuit racing, motocross/supercross/supermoto, trial, enduro, cross-country and track racing. The motorcycling sport-specific extension of the IOC consensus statement aims to provide researchers and governing bodies with a standardised methodology to undertake injury and illness surveillance in motorcycling sport.

records.title: Flexible and stretchable bioelectronics for sports wearable monitoring: Materials, Device Engineering, and Intelligent Wearable Platforms.
records.abstract: Modern sports science is undergoing a paradigm shift from subjective coaching to objective, data-driven precision training. Consequently, wearable electronics for acquiring precise data during sports activities are attracting attention. However, conventional rigid wearables inherently suffer from mechanical mismatches between rigid wearables and the soft, deformable human skin, inducing severe motion artifacts and restricting natural biomechanics during high-intensity athletic activities. To address these limitations from a comprehensive perspective, this review systematically summarizes and analyzes recent advancements in next-generation flexible and stretchable bioelectronics tailored specifically for sports applications. We systematically examine the substrate materials, structural engineering designs, and device-level optimization strategies required to withstand repetitive strain, shear, and sweat-intensive environments. Building upon these conformable bio-interfaces, we discuss three core sensing modalities: electrochemical sensors for real-time analysis of sweat biomarkers, biophysical sensors for continuous electrophysiological and hemodynamic monitoring, and electromechanical sensors for high-fidelity kinematic and impact tracking. Furthermore, we discuss body-derived energy harvesting strategies to power sports wearables and wireless communication systems for continuous athletic monitoring. The importance of artificial intelligence and machine learning is increasing, as these techniques enable the removal of motion artifacts and facilitate objective analysis of athletic data for training and health monitoring applications. By evaluating targeted applications across aerobic and anaerobic exercise, cognitive state assessment, and post-exercise recovery, this review demonstrates how next-generation sports wearables contribute to the shift in sports science from reactive treatment toward proactive, data-driven performance enhancement and injury prevention.

records.title: Gait speed and multi-segment foot joint kinematics throughout the entire stance phase using statistical parametric mapping.
records.abstract: The foot is a multi-segment structure whose segments function together. Due to its ongoing connection with the support surface, the foot must be capable of managing loads that vary with gait speed. Previous studies have provided considerable insight into the relationship between foot joint kinematics and gait speed. However, their primary reliance on discrete measures, such as peak joint angles, has limited understanding of how these relationships evolve throughout the stance phase. The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of gait speed on full time-series trajectories of multiplanar foot joint kinematics using statistical parametric mapping. According to our findings, faster walking primarily increased ankle eversion and midfoot dorsiflexion during weight acceptance (∼17-29% of the stance phase). In contrast, during propulsion, faster walking increased ankle plantar flexion (∼80-100% of the stance phase) and inversion (∼82-90%), as well as midfoot plantar flexion (∼82-100%) and adduction (∼90-98%), together with greater dorsiflexion of the first metatarsophalangeal joint after heel-off (∼43-98% of the stance phase). These multiplanar joint kinematic alterations across the ankle-foot joints throughout the stance phase reflect greater foot-arch collapse in early stance and foot-arch recoil in late stance, which may facilitate appropriate energy absorption and generation in response to increasing gait speed. Importantly, these adaptive foot motions were not captured by previous discrete analyses, which may obscure phase-dependent changes during gait. The present continuous time-series approach revealed detailed temporal adaptations in foot kinematics across the stance phase, providing a more comprehensive characterization of gait mechanics.

records.title: Global research on cricket injuries (1982-2025): A bibliometric analysis.
records.abstract: Cricket is one of the most widely played sports worldwide and carries a significant burden of musculoskeletal injuries, particularly among fast bowlers. Over the past four decades, research in cricket injury epidemiology, biomechanics, workload monitoring, and surveillance has expanded substantially. To conduct a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of global cricket injury research, identifying growth trends, influential publications, leading contributors, collaboration networks, and major thematic domains. Publications from 1982 to 2025 were systematically analyzed using bibliometric indicators including annual growth, authorship productivity, institutional and country contributions, citation impact, total link strength (TLS), and co-authorship networks. The top 100 cited papers and the top 10 highly cited papers (HCPs) were examined in detail to identify landmark contributions and research priorities. A sharp rise in publications occurred after 2003, with nearly 90% of output produced in the last two decades. Australia, the United Kingdom, and South Africa led in productivity, citation impact, and collaborative link strength. The top 10 HCPs accounted for 10% of papers but 37.25% of total citations, underscoring concentrated scholarly influence. Fast bowlers consistently demonstrated the highest injury incidence, particularly lumbar spine and lower limb injuries. Workload spikes were strongly associated with increased injury risk, establishing load monitoring as a central preventive strategy. Biomechanical factors such as mixed bowling action, trunk rotation, and front-knee mechanics were linked to lumbar stress injuries. Standardized injury definitions and international consensus surveillance frameworks significantly improved research quality and comparability. Cricket injury research has evolved into a mature, collaborative, and high-impact domain centered on fast bowling biomechanics, workload regulation, and surveillance standardization. Expanded global participation and integration of advanced analytics are essential for future injury prevention strategies.

records.title: How Effectively Does Protective Sports Gear Prevent Sports Injuries?
records.abstract: As organized and recreational sports continue to grow in popularity, associated sports injuries increasingly burden athletes. Protective sports gear is intended to reduce injury risk during play. This article provides a comprehensive review of the mechanism and efficacy of protective sports gear in injury prevention to the head and neck, upper extremity, and lower extremity and assesses where perhaps evidence for protection is lacking. Helmets, face shields, and protective eyewear have clear benefits in structural protection against injury. The impact of sports gear in reducing sport-related concussion is more variable, largely due to the repetitive nature of the injury mechanism where cumulative low-magnitude impacts contribute to brain injury. For the upper extremity, wrist guards have a clear benefit in reducing major and minor injuries among gymnasts and snowboarders and hence by inference on other impact sports. Ankle braces and taping potentially reduce the risk of ankle sprains among athletes, and the mandating of shin guards in professional soccer results in decreased sports-related lower extremity fractures. Further research is warranted to evaluate the effectiveness of sports gear on reinjury prevention and to study the implications of sports gear on risk compensation theory in athletes.

records.title: Ilizarov Circular Fixation for High-Velocity Firearm Injuries Causing High-Energy Tibial Fractures: A Prospective Cohort Study.
records.abstract: High-velocity gunshot tibial fractures present major reconstructive challenges owing to extensive contamination, soft-tissue devitalisation, and segmental bone loss that render early internal fixation hazardous. We aimed to document outcomes of a structured Ilizarov-based protocol for this injury type and describe a reproducible treatment framework for resource-constrained settings. Between January 2019 and December 2023, we prospectively enrolled 20 adult male patients with open tibial fractures from high-velocity firearm injuries at three Cairo trauma centres; all were treated definitively with an Ilizarov circular external fixator, with distraction osteogenesis and fibular autografting were employed selectively for segmental bone loss. The primary outcome was fracture union rate; secondary outcomes included fixation duration, surgical burden, and complications. Mean age was 29.7 ± 8.4 years. Fourteen fractures (70%) were Gustilo-Anderson type IIIA and six (30%) type IIIB; bone defects were present in 50% after debridement. Union was achieved in 19 of 20 patients (95%), and the single non-union resolved after frame revision and supplementary grafting. Mean fixation duration was 12.3 ± 7.28 months. Superficial pin-tract infection (Checketts-Otterburn Grade 1 or 2) occurred in 17 patients (85%) and deep surgical site infection in one (5%); ankle stiffness, axial malalignment, and limb length discrepancy each affected a minority of patients. structured Ilizarov protocol can reliably achieve union in Gustilo type III gunshot tibial fractures with an acceptable complication profile; these findings are descriptive and do not establish superiority over alternative fixation strategies but support the Ilizarov circular frame as a suitable option for high-grade contaminated injuries in resource-limited environments.

records.title: Injury patterns, in-hospital outcomes, and resource utilization of acute cuboid and navicular fractures.
records.abstract: Acute cuboid and navicular fractures can be serious injuries. However, multicenter data on their associated injuries and in-hospital course are limited. To characterize the demographics, injury patterns, in-hospital outcomes, and resource utilization of trauma center patients with acute cuboid and/or navicular fractures. Retrospective cross-sectional database study. The American College of Surgeons National Trauma Data Bank (2017-2019) was queried for acute cuboid and/or navicular fractures. Multivariable regression identified factors associated with discharge to post-acute care, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, and hospital length of stay in adults. Overall, 3,424 patients with 4,084 fractures were identified (2,327 with cuboid and 1,637 with navicular fractures, including 540 with both). Road-traffic mechanisms accounted for 64.5%, and 25.1% had polytrauma. Metatarsal, calcaneal, and talar fractures were the most common concomitant injuries. Combined fractures were more often ipsilateral than contralateral (457 vs 18 patients). Despite infrequent complications, 50.2% were discharged home without post-acute services (home health, inpatient rehabilitation, or skilled nursing care). In-hospital mortality was 1.1%. After adjustment, polytrauma (OR 3.75, 95% CI 3.04-4.61), bilateral involvement, and ankle, tibia, fibula, or metatarsal fractures were associated with discharge to post-acute care, whereas fracture pattern was not. Cuboid and navicular fractures are predominantly high-energy injuries that rarely occur in isolation. Post-acute care needs, ICU admission, and length of stay were associated with overall injury burden rather than the specific bone fractured.

records.title: Learned helplessness is associated with jump-landing biomechanics following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
records.abstract: Persistent biomechanical alterations following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) contribute to reduced functional performance, increased reinjury risk, and diminished joint health. Rehabilitation emphasizes strength and functional restoration; however, neurobehavioral adaptations may persist. Learned helplessness, characterized by reduced motivation, maladaptive biomechanics, and learned non-use of the reconstructed limb, may relate to post-operative neuromuscular control. However, its relationship with dynamic movement after ACLR remains unclear. This study examined the association between learned helplessness and bilateral lower extremity kinematics during jump-landings in individuals following ACLR. Thirty-three individuals with primary, unilateral ACLR completed a learned helplessness scale and jump-landing task with three-dimensional lower-extremity kinematics. Sagittal and frontal plane knee and hip angles were assessed at initial contact and peak landing. Correlations and regression analyses examined associations with learned helplessness, controlling for age, sex, and time since surgery. Participants were 2.78 ± 2.78 years post-ACLR and demonstrated low helplessness scores. Greater learned helplessness was moderately associated with greater peak knee abduction in the ACLR limb (r = 0.564, p = 0.001). Weak associations were also observed with reduced peak hip flexion in the ACLR (r = -0.370, p = 0.048) and contralateral limbs (r = -0.415, p = 0.025), which did not survive sensitivity analyses. Learned helplessness was independently associated with greater peak knee abduction angle in the ACLR limb (B = 0.230, p = 0.007). The overall model accounted for 34.8% of the variance in peak knee abduction. Learned helplessness appears to be associated with frontal plane knee mechanics following ACLR. Consideration of psychological and neurobehavioral constructs in rehabilitation and return-to-sport assessment following ACLR is important.

records.title: Literature Review of the Utility of Ultrasound for Adolescent and Child Ankle Injuries.
records.abstract: Pediatric posterior ankle pain is a common and challenging presentation due to the complex anatomy and a broad differential diagnosis that includes apophysitis, tendon injuries, fractures, impingement syndromes, infection, and inflammatory arthropathies. Initial evaluation typically consists of physical examination and radiographs, which are often inconclusive and may result in delayed diagnosis, repeat imaging, and/or prolonged immobilization. Magnetic resonance imaging is the gold standard for most of these injuries, but it is expensive and logistically difficult for the pediatric population. A rapid, accessible, and cost-effective imaging modality is needed to improve early detection and management. This review evaluates the role of ultrasound in assessing posterior ankle pathology in pediatric patients. Ultrasound demonstrates high diagnostic accuracy in identifying Achilles tendon tears and differentiating partial- from full-thickness injuries while also assisting in treatment decision making through dynamic tendon gap assessment. It is recommended in several studies for evaluating Achilles tendinopathy and may have predictive value for future symptoms. Emerging evidence supports its adjunctive role in Sever disease and posterior ankle impingement syndrome as well. For osseous and infectious conditions, ultrasound can identify findings suggestive of calcaneal stress fractures, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis. Although magnetic resonance imaging remains the gold standard for these diagnoses, ultrasound improves the detection of joint effusions and synovitis and enhances the accuracy of diagnostic joint aspirations. Overall, ultrasound is a dynamic, radiation-free modality that serves as a powerful adjunctive tool in evaluating pediatric posterior ankle pain.

records.title: Long-term physical health needs of UK military veterans: evaluation of the Op RESTORE health navigation service.
records.abstract: The long-term physical health needs of UK veterans have not been well characterised. Veterans often present with physical health issues attributable to their time in service. Prior to 2016, no dedicated National Health Service (NHS) pathway existed to address these needs. Op RESTORE was established in 2016 to provide coordinated, specialist-led care for veterans with service-attributable physical health conditions. This study describes 10 years of service delivery. A retrospective cross-sectional observational analysis of prospectively collected registry data was performed (2016-2025). Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and statistical comparisons performed against national datasets and between internal subcohorts. A total of 1794 referrals were recorded. Most patients were male Army veterans and presented a median of 15 years after military discharge. Most pathology was non-operational and only 11% of 487 veterans with a documented injury setting had injuries related to combat. Musculoskeletal pathology predominated (79% of 1081 with a confirmed pathway), particularly lower-limb (56%) and spinal injuries (31%). Obesity was highly prevalent (55% of 174 recorded body mass indexes), exceeding national age-matched rates. Mental health comorbidity was common (69%). 64% required navigation to a new clinical pathway. EQ-5D-5L scores improved significantly between referral and discharge from Op RESTORE (p<0.001). Veterans accessing Op RESTORE predominantly present with delayed, chronic musculoskeletal and pain-related morbidity rather than acute combat-related injury. The long interval between military discharge and Op RESTORE presentation highlights a poorly documented and insufficiently monitored progression of service-related pathology over time. This represents missed opportunities for early identification, prevention and intervention. The high burden of multimorbidity and frequent need for specialist triage indicate gaps in standard NHS referral pathways for veterans. Coordinated healthcare navigation addresses unmet need and, in uncontrolled analysis, was associated with improved quality of life. Improved characterisation and longitudinal monitoring of veteran physical health could inform targeted, preventive and integrated service models.

records.title: Lower Body Functional Test Performance Varies Based on Patient Demographics.
records.abstract: The utility of precise and instrumented musculoskeletal performance tests is essential to characterize musculoskeletal function during physical activity. Variation in these tests based on common patient demographics warrants consideration when using test results to counsel and advise physically active people. This study aimed to compare isolated muscle strength and functional performance outcomes by sex (male, female), age (late-stage adolescents: 18-21 years; adults: 22-34 years), and activity level (Tegner Activity Scale {TAS}: TAS ≥7, TAS <7). We hypothesized that males, adults, and individuals with higher activity levels would outperform their dichotomous pair. This is a cross-sectional study. A total of 185 healthy participants (sex: 112 female, 73 male; age: 21±3 years; height: 173±10 cm; mass: 71±12 kg) with no history of lower extremity surgery and no history of lower extremity injury within the previous six months participated in this study. Participants completed isokinetic knee extension/flexion at 90°/s and 180°/s, isometric knee extension/flexion at 90° of knee flexion, the single-leg hop for distance, the triple hop for distance, and the 6-m timed hop. Males, adults, and participants with higher activity levels were stronger than females, late-stage adolescents, and participants with lower activity levels across all isolated muscle strength tests (p<0.05). Males, adults, and participants with higher activity levels jumped farther and faster than females, late-stage adolescents, and participants with lower activity levels for all hop tests except the triple hop for distance. Males, adults, and participants with higher activity levels consistently outperformed females, late-stage adolescents, and participants with lower activity levels, highlighting differences in performance by sex, age, and activity level. These findings suggest that personalization should be considered when using musculoskeletal performance tests to make important healthcare decisions during recovery from injury and/or surgery.

records.title: Male-female differences in unilateral jump-landing energetics are concentrated in propulsion-phase work generation across self-paced and ball-interception tasks in competitive soccer players.
records.abstract: This cross-sectional observational study compared jump performance and braking-, propulsion- and landing-phase energetics during self-paced hands-on-hips single-leg countermovement jump (SL-CMJ) and soccer-relevant jump-heading-landing (SR-JHL) between sampled male and female competitive soccer players. A secondary aim examined associations between propulsion-phase knee positive work (generation) and jump height. Forty-five players (22 males, 18.4 ± 2.1 years; 23 females, 20.1 ± 3.5 years) performed SL-CMJ and SR-JHL bilaterally using force plates and three-dimensional motion capture. SR-JHL incorporated a large-screen interactive soccer scene, real-time marker-driven avatar, unrestricted arms, height-scaled virtual-ball heading and tested-limb landing. Limb-averaged outcomes included jump performance, modified reactive strength index (RSI-mod), phase-specific center-of-mass and hip-knee-ankle work and relative joint contribution. Welch tests, Hedges' g and false discovery rate (FDR) correction compared sexes within tasks; mixed-effects models examined knee energetics-jump height associations. Males had greater jump height and RSI-mod in both tasks (g = 1.34-2.85; q < 0.001), greater propulsion-phase center-of-mass generation and jump center-of-mass net work (g = 0.68-1.35; q ≤ 0.033); however, braking or landing center-of-mass absorption did not differ significantly between groups after FDR correction. Males also showed greater propulsion-phase knee generation, lower ankle generation share, higher knee generation share and greater landing knee absorption. Absolute propulsion-phase knee generation was associated with jump height after accounting for sex and task (β = 0.0147 m per standard deviation; p = 0.042), with a stronger association in SR-JHL (p = 0.006). Differences between the sampled male and female cohorts were concentrated in propulsion-phase work generation, with greater hip and knee work in the male cohort and greater ankle contribution in the female cohort. Propulsion-phase knee positive work was associated with jump height, particularly in SR-JHL. Because sex was inseparable from cohort context, these findings describe between-group differences-not independent sex effects-and provide task-specific comparison context for future anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction and return-to-sport research. Level III.

records.title: Menstrual Cycle Phase-Dependent Lower Extremity Loading Patterns in Adolescent Female Athletes: Implications for Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk.
records.abstract: Physically active females experience substantially higher anterior cruciate ligament injury rates than males, and postmenarche adolescent females commonly demonstrate high-risk mechanics. However, whether mechanics fluctuate across the menstrual cycle remains poorly understood in adolescent female athletes. The aim of this study was to examine differences in lower extremity kinematics and kinetics across two menstrual cycle phases (menstruation and mid-luteal) in postmenarchal adolescent female athletes during a dynamic change-of-direction task. It was hypothesized that biomechanical contributors to dynamic knee valgus would differ between phases. A controlled laboratory study was conducted. Thirty healthy postmenarchal adolescent female athletes (aged 13-17 years) were tested during menstruation (verified by self-reported active bleeding) and mid-luteal phase (scheduled via calendar-based day counting). Kinematics and kinetics were collected using 3-dimensional motion capture and force plates while participants performed a 45° run-cut task. Peak pelvis, hip, and knee angles and hip and knee moments were extracted during the loading phase for each limb. Linear mixed-effects models tested effects of phase and limb dominance (α = 0.05). Participants were aged 15.6 ± 0.9 years, had a height of 168.8 ± 6.2 cm, and weighed 61.2 ± 7.0 kg, and a majority played soccer (70.0%). Compared with menstruation, the mid-luteal phase demonstrated greater peak anterior pelvic tilt (P = .018) and pelvic rise (P = .038), along with reduced peak knee flexion (P = .009). During menstruation, athletes exhibited greater hip abduction moment (P = .037), hip internal rotation moment (P = .043), knee valgus moment (P = .012), and knee external rotation moment (P = .007). Limb dominance effects were observed for pelvic rise (P < .001) and hip internal rotation moment (P = .047). Biomechanical contributors linked to dynamic knee valgus differed by menstrual cycle phase in adolescent female athletes during a change-of-direction task. Menstruation was associated with greater coronal- and transverse-plane hip and knee loading, whereas mid-luteal phase was associated with reduced knee flexion and greater pelvic instability. Cycle-synced injury prevention strategies that are individualized and evidence-based may enhance lower extremity stability when knee control appears most challenged. However, while cycle-synced training may not be feasible in all settings, awareness of phase-related vulnerability may inform screening and load management. (1)Menstrual cycle phase may contribute to variability in lower extremity biomechanics during change-of-direction tasks in adolescent female athletes.(2)Biomechanical risk factors associated with dynamic knee valgus may differ between menstruation and mid-luteal phases.(3)Consideration of menstrual cycle phase may improve interpretation of biomechanical screening and performance testing.(4)Individualized injury prevention strategies may benefit from awareness of phase-related biomechanical changes.
